lead: An X-ray CT scanner never photographs a slice. It fires X-rays through the slice from many angles and measures absorption, so each reading is a line integral of an unknown cross-section f(x,y). Reconstruction turns these line integrals back into a picture. The same idea rebuilds PET and seismic maps. Here reconstruction means building the image from its projections; restoration, the repair of an already-formed blurred image, is a separate topic.
prereq: You need: the degradation model of 3.1 and the 2-D Fourier transform from Unit 2.

sections.h3: The Radon transform and the sinogram

blocks.text: A CT slice is f(x,y): attenuation coefficient in 1/m. A ray is labelled by ρ, signed perpendicular distance from the origin, and θ, angle of that perpendicular from the x axis. Points on the ray satisfy x cos θ + y sin θ = ρ.
R(ρ,θ) = ∫∫ f(x,y) δ(x cos θ + y sin θ − ρ) dx dy
blocks.where: f(x,y) is the object cross-section; θ is the projection angle in radians from the x axis; ρ is the signed perpendicular distance of the ray from the origin, in the same units as x and y; δ is the Dirac delta, zero except where its argument is zero, so the double integral collapses onto the line x cos θ + y sin θ = ρ; R(ρ,θ) is the measured projection value for that ray.

blocks.text: R(ρ,θ) is the total of f along one ray. For fixed θ, R(·,θ) is one view. Stack views as rows to get the sinogram: ray position along one axis, angle along the other. This is the scanner's raw data.

items: Linearity: R of a·f + b·g is a·R_f + b·R_g, because the integral is linear.
Symmetry: R(ρ, θ+π) = R(−ρ, θ). The ray at angle θ+π and distance ρ is the same line as at θ and distance −ρ, so a 360° scan repeats itself. Scanners cover 180° plus the fan width.
A point object at (x₀,y₀) is non-zero only where ρ = x₀ cos θ + y₀ sin θ, so it draws one sine curve in the sinogram.

blocks.text: Take the 1-D Fourier transform of one projection: P_θ(ω) = ∫ R(ρ,θ) e^(−i2πωρ) dρ. The Fourier slice theorem says this is F(u,v) read along one radial line.
P_θ(ω) = F(ω cos θ, ω sin θ)
blocks.where: P_θ(ω) is the 1-D Fourier transform of the projection at angle θ; ω is spatial frequency in cycles per unit length; F(u,v) is the 2-D Fourier transform of f(x,y); the right side is F evaluated at u = ω cos θ and v = ω sin θ.

items: Write P_θ(ω) = ∫ [∫∫ f(x,y) δ(x cos θ + y sin θ − ρ) dx dy] e^(−i2πωρ) dρ.
Swap the order of integration, so the ρ-integral acts on the delta alone.
The delta forces ρ = x cos θ + y sin θ, so e^(−i2πωρ) becomes e^(−i2πω(x cos θ + y sin θ)).
What remains is ∫∫ f(x,y) e^(−i2π(ux+vy)) dx dy with u = ω cos θ and v = ω sin θ, which is F(u,v).

blocks.text: One projection gives one line through the origin of the spectrum. Enough angles fill the frequency plane, and one inverse 2-D transform gives the image.

sections.h3: Filtered back-projection and its digital form

blocks.text: In polar frequency coordinates (ω,θ), du dv becomes ω dω dθ. That factor |ω| is the ramp; it is the Jacobian, not a design choice.
f(x,y) = ∫₀^π Q_θ(x cos θ + y sin θ) dθ,  Q_θ(ρ) = ∫ |ω| P_θ(ω) e^(i2πωρ) dω
blocks.where: |ω| is the ramp filter, the Jacobian of the polar change of variables; Q_θ is the filtered projection at angle θ; ρ = x cos θ + y sin θ selects, for pixel (x,y), the ray passing through it; the outer integral sums the filtered projections over all angles from 0 to π.

blocks.text: Q_θ is the filtered projection: the ramp lifts high frequencies, removing the 1/r blur of plain back-projection. Back-projection then smears each Q_θ along its rays and adds.

items: Sample θ over [0, π) with a step Δθ of about 2/N radians (equivalently about (π/2)N views over 180°) for an N×N image.
Sample ρ at the detector pitch Δρ, one sample per detector channel.
Zero-pad each projection to at least twice its length and take its FFT.
Multiply by the ramp, then inverse FFT, to get Q_θ.
For each pixel, interpolate Q_θ linearly between the two nearest ρ samples, add over all θ, and multiply by Δθ.

blocks.text: Pure |ω| cut at ω_c = 1/(2Δρ) is Ram-Lak. Shepp-Logan multiplies |ω| by a sinc window; Hamming by a raised-cosine window. Both soften the cutoff, trading edge sharpness for less noise.

MRI measures k-space. With gradients on, each readout is one sample of the 2-D Fourier transform of proton density. No line integrals, so no Radon transform. Reconstruction is a 2-D inverse FFT, plus phase and field correction; non-Cartesian trajectories are gridded first.

Same theorem, different door: CT enters through projections and uses FBP; MRI enters through the spectrum and uses inverse FFT. Skipped phase-encode lines leave k-space gaps that partial-Fourier and compressed-sensing methods can fill.

spec.aria: Three 2 by 2 grids. Object f with 1s on the main diagonal and object h with 1s on the other diagonal, each with column sums below, row sums to the left and 45° ray sums at the top right. The back-projection b reads 3 2 / 2 3, total 10.

examples.question: A 2×2 object has f(0,0) = 1, f(1,0) = 0, f(0,1) = 0, f(1,1) = 1, with x and y in pixels. (a) Compute the projections at θ = 0°, 90° and 45°, giving the ray position ρ of each sample. (b) Show that the 0° and 90° views alone cannot separate f from h, where h(1,0) = h(0,1) = 1 and the rest is zero. (c) Compute the unfiltered back-projection b(x,y) using all three views.
steps: θ = 0°: ρ = x. The ray ρ = 0 passes through (0,0) and (0,1), giving R(0,0°) = 1 + 0 = 1. The ray ρ = 1 passes through (1,0) and (1,1), giving R(1,0°) = 0 + 1 = 1.
For h the same two views give column sums 0 + 1 = 1 and 1 + 0 = 1, and row sums 0 + 1 = 1 and 1 + 0 = 1. Both views are identical to f's, so they cannot tell the two objects apart.

θ = 45°: ρ = (x + y)/√2. Ray ρ = 0 through (0,0) gives 1. Ray ρ = 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071 through (1,0) and (0,1) gives 0 + 0 = 0. Ray ρ = √2 ≈ 1.4142 through (1,1) gives 1. For h these three values are 0, 2, 0, which separates the objects.

Back-project: b(x,y) = Σ_θ R(x cos θ + y sin θ, θ). Pixel (0,0) hits ρ = 0, 0, 0, so b = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Pixel (1,0) hits ρ = 1, 0, 0.7071, so b = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Pixel (0,1) hits ρ = 0, 1, 0.7071, so b = 2. Pixel (1,1) hits ρ = 1, 1, 1.4142, so b = 3.

Result: b = [[3,2],[2,3]] against the true f = [[1,0],[0,1]]. The two pixels that should be 0 carry 2 each, and the total is 10 instead of 2. This is the 1/r blur that the ramp filter is there to remove.
examples.answer: b = [[3,2],[2,3]] in the same intensity units as f, a blurred version of f = [[1,0],[0,1]] whose total is 10 instead of 2.

traps: Back-project first and you get the 1/r halo of the example: bright pixels are smeared over the whole image, so the pixel values are wrong and the total is inflated (10 instead of 2 in the example). Filter, then back-project, in that order.
θ in the formulas is in radians, but scanners step in degrees. Convert before you evaluate cos θ and sin θ.
The symmetry R(ρ, θ+π) = R(−ρ, θ) flips the sign of ρ. Folding a 360° scan into [0, π) without the sign flip mirrors half the sinogram.

The ramp |ω| is neither low-pass nor high-pass: it is zero at ω = 0 and rises linearly. It must be band-limited at ω_c = 1/(2Δρ): the sharp-cutoff version is Ram-Lak, and the smoother Shepp-Logan (sinc) and Hamming (raised-cosine) windows trade edge sharpness for less amplified noise.
Filtered back-projection assumes parallel rays. Fan-beam or cone-beam data must be rebinned to parallel geometry, or a fan-beam formula used, before the parallel-beam result applies.

quiz.q: Write the Radon transform and say what ρ and θ mean.
quiz.a: R(ρ,θ) = ∫∫ f(x,y) δ(x cos θ + y sin θ − ρ) dx dy. θ is the ray perpendicular angle from the x axis in radians; ρ is the signed perpendicular distance of the ray from the origin.
P_θ(ω) = F(ω cos θ, ω sin θ): the 1-D Fourier transform of the projection at angle θ equals the 2-D Fourier transform along the radial line at that angle.

quiz.q: Why does the inverse Radon transform contain the factor |ω|?
quiz.a: Polar inversion replaces du dv by ω dω dθ. |ω| is that Jacobian; it removes the 1/r blur of unfiltered back-projection.

quiz.q: Projections are sampled with detector pitch Δρ = 0.5 mm. What cutoff frequency should the ramp filter use?
quiz.a: ω_c = 1/(2Δρ) = 1/(2 × 0.5 mm) = 1 mm⁻¹, that is 1 cycle per millimetre.

quiz.q: A 256×256 image is reconstructed by parallel-beam FBP using about (π/2)N views. How many views are needed, and what is Δθ in degrees?
Too few views produce streak artifacts. Explain why.
quiz.a: Angular sampling below the Nyquist step leaves spectrum radial lines unmeasured. Edges along those directions are unresolved, and the missing frequencies appear as bright and dark streaks.

quiz.q: Why does MRI reconstruction not use the Radon transform?
quiz.a: MRI readouts are already samples of the 2-D Fourier transform, so a 2-D inverse FFT gives the image. No line integrals, no ramp, no back-projection.

beyond: Not for the exam. Clinical CT still uses FBP, but low-dose CT and PET increasingly use iterative reconstruction (ART, SART, MLEM) with regularisers such as total variation. Learned reconstruction replaces the ramp with a trained network. Limited-angle and sparse-view tomography is active research because FBP streaks badly there.
